content.text: Gallstones in the biliary tract (usually in the gallbladder)
: ↑ in Asian population, parasitic, bacterial infections
•OCPs (increased estrogen), Native Americans, bile stasis, chronic hemolysis, cirrhosis, infection, rapid weight loss, IBD, TPN, fibrates, increased triglycerides
Most are asymptomatic – may be an incidental finding
nausea & precipitated by fatty foods or large meals
– initial TOC: stone in GB or cystic duct
: ursodeoxycholic acid may be used to dissolve the gallstones (takes 6-9mo); elective cholecystectomy
Inflammation & infection of the gallbladder due to obstruction of the cystic duct by gallstones
•fibrosis & thickening of the gallbladder due to chronic inflammatory cell infiltration of the gallbladder evident on histopathology –
precipitated by fatty foods or large meals
: RUQ pain or inspiratory arrest w/ palpation of the gallbladder
: referred pain to the right shoulder or subscapular area (phrenic nerve irritation)
: thickened or distended gallbladder, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy’s sign
CT scan: alternative to U/S; can detect complications
: most accurate test – cholecystitis present if there is no visualization of the gallbladder
(can lead to cholestasis due to blockage)
due to the presence of the stone blocking the bile duct
biliary tract infection secondary to obstruction of the common bile duct
diffuse fibrosis of intra/extrahepatic biliary ducts
